title: Behind the Framing
text:
Every news story is shaped by choices about what to emphasise and what to omit. A journalist who chooses a dramatic photograph, a loaded adjective, or a particular opening sentence is already guiding the reader toward a conclusion. Discourse analysts therefore study not only what a text states, but also what it presupposes and what it quietly leaves out.

Critical readers respond to this by interrogating the source before accepting its account. They ask who stands to gain from a given framing, whether the numbers have been separated from their context, and whether opposing views were dismissed too quickly. This scepticism is not the same as cynicism; it is the disciplined habit of treating every persuasive text as a constructed argument rather than a transparent window onto events.

questions.text: According to the first paragraph, what is a journalist doing when choosing a dramatic photograph or a loaded adjective?
options: Guiding the reader toward a conclusion
Checking the facts with official sources
Translating the story into another language
Shortening the article for the printed edition

questions.text: According to the second paragraph, what do critical readers ask about the numbers in a story?
options: Whether they were published in a famous newspaper
Whether they have been separated from their context
Whether they were collected by a government office
Whether they are easy to read in a table

questions.text: What does the author imply about persuasive texts?
options: They should be avoided by careful readers
They are constructed arguments that deserve careful examination
They are harmless when written by experts

questions.text: How does the author separate scepticism from cynicism?
options: Scepticism rejects all evidence, while cynicism accepts it
Scepticism is a disciplined habit of questioning, while cynicism assumes bad intentions
The two words describe exactly the same attitude
Cynicism is a method that discourse analysts require

vocabulary.definition: to give special importance to something
assumes something is true before it is stated
questioning someone or something closely and carefully
a habit of questioning claims before accepting them

paragraph_translations: Cada noticia está moldeada por decisiones sobre qué enfatizar y qué omitir. Un periodista que elige una fotografía dramática, un adjetivo cargado de intención o una frase de apertura particular ya está guiando al lector hacia una conclusión. Por eso, los analistas del discurso estudian no solo lo que un texto afirma, sino también lo que presupone y lo que deja fuera en silencio.

Los lectores críticos responden a esto interrogando a la fuente antes de aceptar su versión. Preguntan quién se beneficia de un encuadre determinado, si las cifras han sido separadas de su contexto y si las opiniones contrarias fueron descartadas demasiado rápido. Este escepticismo no es lo mismo que el cinismo; es el hábito disciplinado de tratar cada texto persuasivo como un argumento construido y no como una ventana transparente a los hechos.
